lead: Landing gear and flaps must move only when the aircraft is in the right state, and the stall system watches angle of attack so it can warn, and if needed act, before lift is lost. Gear control commands up or down, checks the locks and shows the result; flap control drives the flaps to each selected step and stops them if the two wings disagree; the stall computer compares angle of attack with a limit that depends on the flap setting, shakes the stick as a warning and, on some types, pushes it as protection.
prereq: You need: landing gear and brakes for the gear structure, hydraulic systems for actuation, and the air data instruments topic for airspeed.

blocks.text: The gear lever sends an electrical command to the gear control unit (on the A320 family, two landing gear control and interface units working in turn). The unit opens a selector valve: for retraction it first opens the doors, unlocks the downlocks, retracts the legs into the uplocks, then closes the doors; extension runs the other way. Proximity sensors, which detect a metal target without touching it, tell the unit when each lock and door has reached position, and it moves to the next step only then.

A squat switch (weight-on-wheels sensor) on the shock strut senses that the strut is compressed. On the ground it blocks retraction, even if the lever is moved up, and it switches many systems between ground and flight logic. Position sensors drive the indication: three green lamps for down and locked, red for in transit or disagreeing with the lever, and nothing when the gear is up and locked. A press-to-test button checks the lamps.

The gear warning sounds when the gear is not down and locked and the throttles are near idle at low height, the usual sign of an approach. On many types it also sounds when the flaps are set for landing with the gear not down, and that warning cannot be silenced. High power with the gear up does not trigger it, so the crew must still check the green lamps.

If hydraulic pressure is lost, alternate extension releases the uplocks, by a cable, an electric motor or a gas bottle, and the gear falls under its own weight. The air load and assist springs push the legs into the downlocks.

sections.h3: Flap selection, asymmetry and load limiting

blocks.text: Trailing-edge Fowler flaps move aft and down, adding area and camber. The flap lever has detents such as UP, 1, 2, 3 and FULL. On a transport the lever position goes to a flap control computer, which runs a central power drive unit. That unit has two motors (two hydraulic, or one hydraulic and one electric) driving torque shafts that run along each wing to a ball-screw or rotary actuator at every flap track. Position pick-offs (synchros or rotary transducers) at the drive unit and at the wing tips report where the flaps are, and the computer stops the drive when they match the lever. On a light aircraft an electric motor, limit switches and a position indicator do the same job.

Both wings must move together. The computer compares the left and right wing-tip pick-offs: if they differ by more than a small threshold (an asymmetry), it stops the drive and sets the wing-tip brakes, which lock the torque shafts. A skew sensor finds one flap panel out of line with its neighbour on the same wing, for example after a track or actuator failure, and also stops the drive. A split flap would roll the aircraft, so stopping is safer than finishing the selection.

Load limiting protects the structure. At high airspeed the air load on extended flaps is large, so on some types the computer retracts the flaps one step automatically above the placard speed (flap load relief) and runs them out again when the speed falls. Limit switches also stop the drive at full up and full down.

Angle of attack α is the angle between the wing chord line and the relative airflow. Lift rises with α until the wing stalls at the critical angle, so a stall depends on α, not on speed alone: an aircraft can stall at high speed in a steep turn. For level flight the stall speed is:

blocks.where: V<sub>S</sub> is the stall speed in m/s; W is the weight in N; ρ is the air density in kg/m³; S is the wing area in m²; C<sub>Lmax</sub> is the maximum lift coefficient, which rises when flaps are extended. Certification rules require the stall warning to begin at least 5 kt or 5 % above the stall speed, whichever is greater.

blocks.text: On a light aircraft the warning comes from a small flapper switch on the wing leading edge: near the stall the stagnation point moves down and back, the airflow lifts the flapper and the switch sounds a horn. Some trainers use a reed horn instead, sounded by air sucked through a slot. Transports use an angle of attack vane on the fuselage side, a small weathervane whose rotary transducer sends α to the stall warning computer, which also receives flap and slat position and Mach number from the air data computer, because the stall angle changes with both.

Near the stall angle the computer drives the stick shaker, an electric motor turning an unbalanced weight on the control column, often with a horn or voice call. The shaker is a warning: it tells the crew to lower the nose.

Types whose stall is hard to recover, such as many T-tail jets, add a stick pusher: at a higher α an actuator pushes the column forward to reduce α even if the crew delays. Because a pusher acting wrongly is itself a hazard, it is inhibited on the ground by the squat switch, needs both α channels to agree, and can be cut out by the crew. Fly-by-wire aircraft go further: alpha protection limits α in the flight control laws, and alpha floor commands full thrust.

The scale shows the worked example: the same aircraft stalls at 145.1 kt clean but 106.2 kt with full flap, so the warning limit must change with flap; with full flap it may not start below 111.5 kt.

examples.question: An airliner of mass 64 000 kg has a wing area of 122.6 m². At sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³) its C<sub>Lmax</sub> is 1.5 clean and 2.8 with full flap. Take g = 9.81 m/s² and 1 kt = 0.5144 m/s. Find the stall speed in each configuration, and the lowest speed at which the stall warning may start with full flap.
steps: Warning margin with full flap: 5 % of 106.2 = 5.3 kt, which is more than 5 kt, so the margin is 5.3 kt.
examples.answer: The stall speed is 145.1 kt clean and 106.2 kt with full flap; the warning must start at 111.5 kt or above. The stall computer needs flap position because the same α limit does not fit both configurations.

traps: Do not swap the stick shaker and stick pusher. The shaker warns; the pusher acts.
The gear warning needs gear not down plus throttles at idle, or landing flap; gear up at high power does not sound it.
A squat switch is not a lock switch. It senses weight on the strut; lock and door positions come from proximity sensors.
Asymmetry compares left with right wing; skew compares panels on the same wing. Both stop the drive.
Stall speed varies as √W, so a heavier aircraft stalls faster: 20 % more weight gives √1.2 = 1.095, about 9.5 % more speed.

quiz.q: What does the stick shaker do?
quiz.a: It vibrates the control column as a stall warning, near the stall angle of attack.

quiz.q: State two functions of the gear downlock sensors.
quiz.a: They confirm down and locked and light the green lamps. They tell the control unit the extension is complete so it can close the doors and remove pressure, and they feed the gear warning.

quiz.q: Why does flap asymmetry protection stop both flaps instead of driving the lagging flap to catch up?
quiz.a: The cause may be a broken shaft or jammed actuator, so the lagging side may never catch up. Stopping both drives and setting the wing-tip brakes holds the asymmetry small, and the roll it causes stays within aileron control.

quiz.q: An aircraft of 60 000 kg stalls at 130 kt. Using V<sub>S</sub> ∝ √W, find the stall speed at 48 000 kg.
Why is a stick pusher inhibited on the ground and given a crew cut-out?
quiz.a: A pusher that fires wrongly forces the nose down. On the ground, a faulty vane could push during the take-off rotation, so weight-on-wheels logic inhibits it; in flight a channel failure could push at low height, so the crew must be able to disconnect it and the two α channels must agree before it acts.

quiz.q: On final approach with the gear up, the throttles are well above idle and the horn is silent. Is the system faulty?
quiz.a: Not necessarily. The throttle-based warning needs low power; at higher power it stays quiet. But if landing flap is selected, many types sound a warning that cannot be silenced, so silence then would be a fault. The crew must check the three green lamps.

quiz.q: How does a flap control computer know when to stop the drive?
quiz.a: Position pick-offs at the drive unit send the flap position; when it matches the lever detent the computer stops the motors and applies the drive brake. In simple light-aircraft systems a limit switch breaks the motor circuit itself.

beyond: Not for the exam. Fly-by-wire airliners blend stall protection into the control laws (alpha protection, alpha floor). Research looks at synthetic angle of attack from inertial and air data, so one faulty vane cannot fool the system. Search for "angle of attack limiting", "flap asymmetry protection" and "stick pusher".
